ELECTIVE AREA

ELECTIVE AREA 3 · JUNE

Tilings

Tiles in the bathroom, paving on the pavement, cells in a beehive: here identical shapes cover a surface without gaps and without overlaps. In this elective area you find out which polygons form a tiling and why others do not fit. Then you turn a square into a tile of your own – just like the artist M. C. Escher.

8 LESSONS2 UNITS2 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • check whether a polygon can be laid into a tiling: the angles at every vertex add up to 360°
  • find tilings made of regular polygons, also of two kinds
  • explain why every triangle and every quadrilateral tiles, but the regular pentagon does not
  • design tilings of your own after M. C. Escher with templates

UNIT 14 LESSONS

1Tilings with polygons

Where several pieces of a tiling meet, their angles lie around one point. Around a point there are exactly 360°. So a tiling only works if the angles at every vertex add up to 360°.

For regular polygons of one kind, 360° must be divisible by the interior angle. That only works for triangles ($6 \cdot 60^\circ$), squares ($4 \cdot 90^\circ$) and hexagons ($3 \cdot 120^\circ$). With two kinds there are more tilings, for example of octagons and squares.

Every triangle tiles: two identical triangles make a parallelogram. And every quadrilateral tiles, even a skewed one: the four angles add up to 360°, and you keep turning it by 180° about the midpoint of a side.

KEY POINT · TILING

Tiling: without gaps, without overlaps · at every vertex the angles add up to $360^\circ$

Regular, one kind: only triangle, square, hexagon

Always possible: with every triangle and with every quadrilateral · not possible: with the regular pentagon ($3 \cdot 108^\circ = 324^\circ$)

Notation: “4.8.8” means: a square and two octagons meet at every vertex.

In space: if there is less than 360° at a vertex, you can fold the net into a corner – that is how solids come about.

INTERACTIVE · TILINGS WITH REGULAR POLYGONS

Choose a tiling. On the right you see which angles meet at a vertex. Why does it not work with pentagons?

OUTLOOK · LESS THAN 360° AT A VERTEX

Lay regular polygons around a vertex. If the sum is less than 360°, a corner in space can be folded.

EXAMPLE 1 · OCTAGONS AND SQUARES

Why do regular octagons on their own not form a tiling, but they do together with squares?

Interior angle of the octagon: $1080^\circ : 8 = 135^\circ$. Two octagons: $270^\circ$, three: $405^\circ$ – that never fits. With a square: $270^\circ + 90^\circ = 360^\circ$.

tiling 4.8.8

EXAMPLE 2 · DODECAGONS

Which regular polygon fits at a vertex together with two regular dodecagons?

Dodecagon: $(12 - 2) \cdot 180^\circ : 12 = 150^\circ$. Two: $300^\circ$, $60^\circ$ are missing.

a triangle – tiling 3.12.12

EXERCISES

Calculate the interior angle of the regular 3-, 4-, 5-, 6- and 8-gon. For which is 360° divisible by the interior angle?

60°, 90°, 108°, 120°, 135°. Divisible only for 60° (6 of them), 90° (4) and 120° (3).

Draw any triangle on squared paper and lay a tiling from it (at least 8 triangles). How many triangles meet at a vertex?

Six: each of the three angles occurs twice, $2 \cdot (\alpha + \beta + \gamma) = 360^\circ$.

Three triangles and two squares at a vertex: does that work? Is there another mixture of regular triangles and squares?

$3 \cdot 60^\circ + 2 \cdot 90^\circ = 360^\circ$ – yes. Other mixtures: only the same numbers in a different order (3.3.4.3.4).

Draw a skewed quadrilateral on card, cut out 6 of them and lay a tiling. How do you have to turn the quadrilaterals?

Each neighbouring quadrilateral comes from a half turn (180°) about the midpoint of the common side. At each vertex all four angles lie together, 360° in total.

Explain why there is no tiling with regular heptagons, not even together with other regular polygons at a vertex with two heptagons.

Interior angle ≈ 128.6°. Three are ≈ 385.7° – too much. Two are ≈ 257.1°, ≈ 102.9° are missing. No regular polygon has this angle (triangle 60°, square 90°, pentagon 108°), and two smaller angles do not fit either (60° + 60° = 120°).

TEST YOURSELF!

Three regular pentagons at a vertex: how big is the gap?

$360 - 324 = 36$

Interior angle in a regular dodecagon?

$1800 : 12 = 150$

How many equilateral triangles meet at a vertex?

$360 : 60 = 6$

UNIT 24 LESSONS

2Tilings after M. C. Escher

The Dutch graphic artist Maurits Cornelis Escher (1898–1972) filled surfaces with birds, fish and lizards that interlock without any gaps. His trick: he started with a polygon that tiles and changed the edges by fixed rules.

With a translation, you cut a piece out of one side of a square and stick it back on exactly opposite. The tile then still fits its neighbours. If you do that with both pairs of sides, you get a shape from which you can draw an animal.

With a rotation, you cut a piece off one side and turn it about a vertex onto the neighbouring side. That way too the tile still tiles.

KEY POINT · ESCHER TILES

Basic shape: a polygon that tiles (square, rectangle, parallelogram, hexagon, triangle)

Translating: move the change of one side onto the opposite side · rotating: turn the change about a vertex or the midpoint of a side

The area stays the same: what is taken away is added somewhere else.

Alhambra: in 1936 Escher visited the palace in Granada and copied the Moorish tile patterns. After that he began his tessellations.

If you are interested: from Escher patterns you can fold kaleidocycles, rings of tetrahedra that can be turned endlessly.

INTERACTIVE · YOUR ESCHER TILE

Drag the red and the purple point. The tile changes – and still fills the surface without gaps.

EXAMPLE 3 · A TEMPLATE BY TRANSLATION

How do you make a template from a square with a 6 cm side?

1. Cut a shape out of the left side. 2. Move it unchanged to the right and stick it to the right side. 3. The same with the bottom and the top side. 4. Draw round the template again and again, shifted each time.

The area stays 36 cm²

EXAMPLE 4 · HOW MANY TILES?

An Escher tile is made from a square with a 5 cm side. How many tiles do you need for a poster of 1 m × 0.5 m?

Each tile has 25 cm², the poster 5000 cm².

200 tiles

EXERCISES

Use the interactive element to design a tile that looks like a fish. Describe which edges you changed.

For example: left edge bent to the right (the right one follows), bottom edge bent upwards (the top one follows). The eye and the fins are drawn in.

A tile is made from a rectangle of 4 cm × 3 cm. How big is its area, no matter how the edges were changed?

12 cm² – translation does not change the area.

Make a template by translation from card and use it to draw a tiling of at least 12 tiles. Colour it in two alternating colours.

Your own result. Check: there must be neither gaps nor overlaps.

Why does it not work if you reflect the cut-out piece onto the opposite side instead of moving it?

Then the bulge on one side points outwards, and on the neighbouring tile it also points outwards at the same place – they overlap, and somewhere else a gap is left.

Try the rotation: cut a piece out of the bottom side of a square and turn it by 90° about the bottom left vertex onto the left side. Lay four tiles around this vertex to make a square. What do you notice?

Four tiles, each turned by 90° about the common vertex, fit together without gaps. This creates patterns with rotational symmetry, as with Escher’s lizards.

TEST YOURSELF!

An Escher tile from a square with a 6 cm side: area in cm²?

$6 \cdot 6 = 36$

Tiles from 5 cm squares for 1 m × 0.5 m?

$5000 : 25 = 200$

A tile from a rectangle of 4 cm × 3 cm: area in cm²?

$12$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

A bathroom is tiled with hexagonal tiles. How many tiles meet at a vertex? How big is each angle there?

3 tiles of 120° each.

A pavement is 1.5 m wide and 20 m long. It is paved with square slabs with a 30 cm side. How many slabs do you need?

$150 : 30 = 5$ across, $2000 : 30 \approx 66.7$ lengthwise, so 67 rows: 335 slabs (some are cut to size).

A tiling consists of regular hexagons, squares and triangles: at every vertex there are one hexagon, two squares and one triangle. Check the angle sum.

$120^\circ + 2 \cdot 90^\circ + 60^\circ = 360^\circ$ ✓ (the tiling 3.4.6.4).

EXCURSIONRESEARCH

Pentagons that do fit

The regular pentagon does not tile. But there are irregular convex pentagons that can – the mathematician Karl Reinhardt showed this as early as 1918. How many kinds there are remained open for almost a hundred years.

In 1975 Martin Gardner wrote about the known kinds in a magazine. Marjorie Rice, a homemaker from San Diego, read the article, invented a notation of her own and found four new kinds at her kitchen table. In 2015 three researchers in the USA discovered the 15th kind with the computer.

In 2017 the Frenchman Michaël Rao proved with a computer search: there are exactly these 15 kinds of convex pentagons that tile the plane – no more.

Sources: Karl Reinhardt, doctoral thesis, Frankfurt 1918; Martin Gardner, “Mathematical Games”, Scientific American, July 1975; Casey Mann, Jennifer McLoud-Mann, David Von Derau, 2015; Michaël Rao, “Exhaustive search of convex pentagons which tile the plane”, 2017.
